title: Incremental Hydration
description: Learn about incremental hydration in Angular with @defer blocks: triggers (idle, viewport, interaction, hover, immediate, timer, when, never) and performance benefits.

blocks.text: Incremental hydration is an advanced type of hydration that can leave sections of your application dehydrated and incrementally trigger hydration of those sections as they are needed.
Incremental hydration builds on top of full-application hydration, deferrable views (@defer), and event replay.
Why use incremental hydration?
Incremental hydration provides substantial performance improvements:

items: Smaller initial bundles: Produces smaller initial JavaScript bundles while providing an experience comparable to full application hydration.
Better Core Web Vitals: Improves initial load times, reducing First Input Delay (FID / INP) and Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS).
Above-the-fold deferrable views: You can now use @defer blocks above the fold without layout shift because the main template renders directly on the server without placeholder swapping on the client.

blocks.text: How do you enable incremental hydration in Angular?
Incremental hydration is enabled by default when you use provideClientHydration():
Incremental Hydration depends on and enables event replay automatically. If you already have withEventReplay() in your list, you can safely remove it.
Opting out of incremental hydration
To opt out of incremental hydration, use withNoIncrementalHydration():
How does incremental hydration work?

Adding a hydrate trigger to a defer block tells Angular to load dependencies during SSR and render the main template rather than the @placeholder. On client-side initial load, dependencies remain deferred and the defer block content stays dehydrated until its hydrate trigger fires. Browser events triggered prior to hydration are queued and replayed upon completion.
Controlling hydration of content with triggers
There are three types of hydrate triggers: hydrate on, hydrate when, and hydrate never.
hydrate on

rows: Triggers when the browser is idle. Supports an optional timeout.
Triggers when specified content enters the viewport.
Triggers when the user interacts with specified element.
Triggers when the mouse hovers over specified area.
Triggers immediately after non-deferred content has finished rendering.

blocks.text: hydrate when
The hydrate when trigger accepts a custom conditional expression and hydrates when the condition becomes truthy.
hydrate never
hydrate never specifies that the content in the defer block should remain dehydrated indefinitely on initial load, effectively becoming static content.
Hydrate triggers alongside regular triggers
Hydration is an initial load optimization, meaning hydrate triggers apply to the initial load, while subsequent client-side renders use regular triggers:
Nested @defer blocks

Because Angular's component architecture is hierarchical, hydrating any component requires all of its parents also be hydrated. Hydration is triggered from the top-most dehydrated @defer block down to the triggered child.
Do I still need to specify @placeholder blocks?
Yes. While @placeholder content is not used for incremental hydration during initial SSR load, it is still necessary for subsequent client-side navigation renders.
